translations.text: Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, saying: and so on.

"The Lord was speaking at a certain time to his apostles in parables, saying thus: The kingdom of heaven is like a certain king who made a marriage feast for his son. Then he sent his heralds to invite his subjects:" and so on.
In this reading we follow the exposition of Pope Gregory.
My dearest brothers, I have often told you that everywhere in the holy gospel this present Church is called the kingdom of heaven.

Truly, the gathering of righteous people is called the kingdom of heaven. God said through his prophet, "Heaven is my throne." Paul the Apostle said that "Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God."

We can clearly understand that the soul of every righteous person is heaven, since Christ is the Wisdom of God, and the soul of a righteous person is the throne of that wisdom, and heaven is his throne.
Of this the psalmist said, "The heavens declare the glory of God." He called God's heralds heavens.

Truly, the congregation of holy people is the kingdom of heaven, because their hearts are not caught up in earthly desires; instead they yearn for the things above. God already reigns in them now, as in heavenly dwellings.
The king who made the marriage feast for his son is God the Father, who joined the holy Church to his Son through the mystery of his incarnation.
The holy Church is Christ's bride, through whom he begets spiritual children every day, and she is the mother of all Christian people, and yet an undefiled virgin.
Through faith and baptism we are begotten to God and adopted as his spiritual children, through Christ's humanity and through the grace of the Holy Spirit.
God sent his messengers to invite everyone to this marriage feast. He sent once, and again;

for he sent his prophets, who proclaimed that his Son's incarnation was to come, and afterwards he sent his apostles, who proclaimed that his coming had been accomplished, just as the prophets had prophesied it before.
When they would not come to the wedding, he sent again, saying:
"Tell those who are invited: Behold, I have prepared my good things, I have slaughtered my bulls and my fattened birds, and I have made all my things ready. Come to the wedding."
The bulls signify the patriarchs of the old law, who were then permitted, by leave of the old law, to slay their enemies in the manner of bulls.
It is written thus in the old law: "Love your friend, and hate your enemy."
Thus it was permitted to the people of old that they might subdue God's adversaries and their own enemies with strong might, and kill them with weapons.
But the same God who gave this permission through the law of Moses before his coming, that same God, when he afterwards came into the world in human nature, changed that saying, speaking thus:
"I command you: love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you, and pray for your persecutors, so that you may be children of the heavenly Father,
who lets his sun shine on the good and the evil, and gives showers of rain and crops to the righteous and the unrighteous." What do the bulls signify but the fathers of the old law?
What were they but like bulls, when, by leave of the old law, they butted their enemies with the horn of bodily might?
The fattened birds signify the holy teachers of the New Testament.
They are so greatly fattened with the grace of the Holy Spirit that they long for the journey upward on the wings of a spiritual way of life.
What is it for a person to set his thought on lowly things but a kind of leanness of mind? He who is filled with the food of heavenly love is as if he were fattened with abundant food.
With this fatness the psalmist wished to be fattened when he said, "Let my soul be filled as with fat and with suet."
What does "My oxen are slain, and my fatted fowls" mean, unless it is as if he said, 'Look at the way of life of the patriarchs,
and understand the prophets' singing and the apostles' preaching about my Son's humanity, and come to the wedding'?
That is, 'Come with faith, and join yourselves to the holy Church, which is his bride and your mother.'
"They neglected it and went off, some to their farms, some to their trade."
He goes to his farm and despises God's preparation who works at earthly tillage beyond measure, so much that he neglects his share in God.
He goes about his trading who, with greed for worldly treasures, bargains more eagerly for them than for the riches of eternal life.
Truly, when some of them busy themselves beyond all bounds with earthly tillage, and some with worldly hoards, then because of that busyness they cannot think about the Saviour's humanity;
And it also seems very burdensome to them that they should make their habits conform to his rule.
Some are also so perversely minded that they cannot listen to God's preaching, but afflict God's messengers with persecution, as the gospel says further on:
"Some of them seized the messengers, tormented them with insults, and killed them. But when the king learned of this, he sent his army there, destroyed the murderers, and burned their city."
He destroyed the murderers, because he cruelly killed the wicked persecutors, as we read everywhere in the passions of the martyrs.
Nero, the cruel emperor, ordered Peter to be crucified and Paul to be beheaded, but he was suddenly driven out of his kingdom, and wolves tore him to pieces.

Herod beheaded the apostle James, and put Peter in prison; but God rescued him from his captivity, and while the king was pondering how he had got out of the prison, God's angel came to him afterwards and struck him dead.
Astyages, the Indian king who slew Bartholomew, went mad, and died in that madness. Likewise Aegeas, who crucified Andrew, ended straightaway in madness.
It would take long to recount the ends of all the impious persecutors, how fiercely Almighty God avenged on them the sufferings of his saints.
The gospel says that he burned up their city, because they will be burned in eternal torment, both in soul and in body.
"He sent his army," because he destroys the wicked through his angels. What are the hosts of angels but the army of the Heavenly King?
He is called Dominus Sabaoth, that is, 'Lord of the Army,' or 'Lord of Hosts.'
The king then said to his servants, "This wedding is ready, but those whom I invited to it were not worthy of it.
"Go now to the outlets of the roads, and whomever you find, invite to the wedding." The roads are the various deeds of men.
The outlets of the roads are the failing of worldly works; and those very often come to God who prosper little in earthly works.
So the king's messengers went along the roads, gathering all whom they found, both bad and good, and filled the wedding completely.
In this present Church bad and good are mixed, just as clean grain with foul cockle:
but at the end of this world the true Judge will command his angels to gather the cockle in bundles and throw it into the unquenchable fire.
They gather the sinful from the righteous in bundles, when murderers are bound together in the fire of hell, thieves with thieves, the greedy with the greedy, fornicators with fornicators;
and so all wicked companions suffer together, bound up in the eternal torments; and the clean wheat is brought into God's barn.
that is, that the righteous will be brought to eternal life, where no storm comes nor any bad weather to harm the grain.
Then the good will be nowhere but in heaven, and the wicked nowhere but in hell.
My brothers, if you are good, then you must patiently bear with the wickedness of reprobate people for as long as you remain in this present life.
He who will not bear with an evil person is not good. Concerning this, God's voice said to the prophet Ezekiel:
"You, son of man, unbelievers and those who incite to evil are with you, and you dwell among the worst kind of serpents."
Again, Paul the Apostle praised and strengthened the life of believing people, urging them thus: "Live among a perverse mankind; shine among them as stars, holding fast the word of life."
"The king went in and looked over the guests, and there he saw a man who was not clothed in a wedding garment." The wedding garment stands for the true love of God and of other people.
Our Creator showed us that love through himself, when he deigned to redeem us from eternal death with his precious blood, just as John the Evangelist said,
"God loved this world so much that he gave his only-begotten Son for us." The Son of God, who came to humankind through love, indicated in the gospel what the wedding garment signified: true love.
Everyone who turns to God with faith and baptism comes to the wedding; but he does not come in a wedding garment if he does not hold to true love.
Truly, you see that anyone who is invited to a worldly wedding is ashamed to come shabbily dressed to that brief joy;
but much greater shame awaits the one who comes to God's wedding in a filthy garment, so that because of his foul clothing he is thrust out of the eternal joy into eternal darkness.
Just as clothing makes a person beautiful in body, so true love also makes our soul beautiful with spiritual fairness.
Even if a person has full faith, gives alms, and does much good, whatever he does is all in vain for him unless he has true love for God and for all Christian people.
True love is this: that each person loves his friend in God and his enemy for God's sake.
Every day the Heavenly King goes into the wedding, that is, into his Church, and looks to see whether we are clothed inwardly in the wedding garment;
And anyone he finds without true love he questions angrily, saying, "Friend, how did you dare to come to my feast without a wedding garment?"
He called him "friend", and yet he cast him out from among his guests. He was a friend through faith, and an enemy through his works.
He was struck dumb at once, because at God's judgment there is no excuse and no contradiction; the Judge who rebukes from outside is a witness to the man's conscience within.
Though someone does not yet perfectly have true love, he should not despair of himself, because the prophet said to God concerning such people:
"My Lord, your eyes have seen my imperfection, and all are written in your book."
The king said to his servants, "Bind the badly clothed man hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."
The hands and feet that are not bound now by the fear of God, keeping them from perverse deeds, will then be bound fast by the severity of God's judgment.
The feet that refuse to visit the sick and the hands that give nothing to the poor will then be bound in punishment, because they are now bound away from good works of their own free will.
The badly clothed man was thrown into the outer darkness. The inner darkness is the blindness of the heart. The outer darkness is the black night of eternal damnation.

The damned man, then, suffers in the outer darkness by compulsion, because now he willingly spends his life in the blindness of his heart and has no remembrance of the true light, that is, Christ, who said of himself:
"I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness, but has the light of life." In the outer darkness there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
There the eyes that now wander about gazing through unlawful desires will weep in the hellish flame;
and the teeth that now delight in gluttony shall gnash there in the unspeakable torments that are prepared for God's adversaries.
Truly, the eyes will stream with tears because of the intense smoke, and the teeth will chatter because of the great cold, for the reprobate suffer unbearable heat and unspeakable cold.
Truly, the fire of hell has unspeakable heat and no light, but burns forever in black darkness.
If anyone has doubts about the resurrection, he can understand from this gospel that there will be a true resurrection, since there will be eyes and teeth there.
Eyes are of flesh and teeth are of bone, because, whether we wish it or not, we must rise at the end of this world with flesh and with bone, and receive the reward of all our deeds,
either a dwelling with God for good merits, or the torment of hell with the devil for wicked deeds. Concerning this the blessed Job said:
"I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, I myself, and not another."
That is, not another form in my place, but I myself shall see him.
The ending of this gospel is very fearful: "Many are called, and few are chosen."
Look: the voice of all of us now calls on Christ, but the life of all of us does not call on him; for many contradict by their conduct what they profess with their voice.
Some people make a good beginning for a while, but they end in evil. Some make an evil beginning, and end well through true repentance. Some begin well, and end better.
So everyone should greatly fear for himself, even if he leads a good life, and in no way be overconfident about himself; for he does not know whether he is worthy to enter the eternal kingdom.
Nor should he despair of others, even if they fall into sins; for he does not know the manifold riches of God's mercy.
Now Saint Gregory says that a certain brother turned to a monastery that he himself had founded, and after the trial prescribed by the rule he took the monastic habit.
A brother of his by blood followed him to the monastery, not out of zeal for a good way of life, but out of fleshly affection.
The spiritual brother greatly pleased all the monks of the monastery through his good conduct, while his brother by blood strongly and perversely opposed his way of life.
He lived in the monastery out of necessity rather than to better himself. He was frivolous in speech and perverse in his deeds, well dressed in clothing and evil in his habits.
He had no patience if anyone urged him toward a good way of life. So his life became very burdensome to the brothers, but they bore it patiently for the sake of his brother's goodness.
He could not do anything good, and he would not listen to anything good. Then he was suddenly struck by a certain disease and brought to the point of death.
When he was brought to the point of departure, the brothers came to commend his soul.
He lay with his lower limbs gone cold; only in his breast did the spirit still breathe.
The brothers then prayed for him all the more earnestly, as they saw that he was soon to die. Then he suddenly cried out, saying:
"Go away from me. Behold, a dragon has come here that is to swallow me, but he cannot because of your presence. He has seized my head in his jaws.
Make room for him, so that he may torment me no longer. If I have been given to this dragon to be swallowed, why must I suffer delay because of your standing over me?"
The brothers said to him, "Why do you speak with such great despair? Mark yourself with the sign of the holy cross."
He answered as well as he could, "I would gladly bless myself with the sign of the holy cross, but I do not have the strength, because the dragon is pressing hard on me."
So the monks prostrated themselves on the ground with weeping, and began to pray more earnestly to the ruling God for his deliverance.
Then suddenly the sick youth recovered, and said in a joyful voice,
"I thank God: see, now the dragon that wanted to swallow me has been put to flight because of your prayers. He has been driven away from me, and could not stand against your intercession."
Be my intercessors now, praying for my sins; for I am ready to turn to the monastic way of life and give up all worldly habits."
Then his cold limbs came back to life, and he turned to God with all his heart. Through a long illness he was set right in his conversion, and at last he died of that same illness;
but he did not see the dragon at his death, because he had overcome it by turning his heart to God.
We should not despair, even though in this present Church many are evil and few are good;
for Noah's ark on the waves of the great flood was a symbol of this Church, and it was wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.
On the lowest deck lived the fierce beasts and creeping serpents. On the second floor lived birds and clean animals.
On the third floor lived Noah with his wife, and his three sons with their three wives.
At the bottom, where the fierce beasts lived, the ark was roomy, and higher up, where the people lived, it was narrowed;
for the holy Church is very broad in carnal people and narrow in spiritual ones.
She spreads out her bosom where the fierce live in beastly ways, and she is narrowed at the end where the rational live, conducting themselves in spiritual ways;
for the holier they are in this present Church, the fewer of them there are.
There are far more people who live according to their own desires than there are who set right the conduct of their lives according to God's commandments;
nevertheless, the number of holy people is always increased through the dwindling of the wicked. The number of God's chosen is not small, just as Christ said in another place,
"Many will come from the east and from the west, and will sit with the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven."
Again, the psalmist said of God's chosen ones, "I counted them, and their number is greater than the sand."

In this present life the chosen seem few compared with the number of the rejected. But when they are gathered into eternal life, their number will be so great that, as the prophet said, it will be more than the grains of sand.
Lead us, Almighty God, to the number of your chosen saints, into the eternal bliss of your kingdom,
which you have prepared from the beginning of the world for those who love you, you who live and reign with the Eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
